title: How the Web Works
eyebrow: Foundation · One address-bar request from start to finish
summary: Follow what actually happens after you enter a web address: the browser finds the destination, creates a protected connection, asks for resources, receives a response, and turns the result into a page.
aliases: what happens when I open a website
learningOutcomes: Trace a page load from the address bar to the server and back to the screen.
Explain what DNS, the network connection, TLS, HTTP, and browser rendering each do without mixing their jobs together.
Use the earliest failing stage to narrow down common website-loading problems.

heroVisual.title: A page load is a chain of handoffs
heroVisual.caption: Each stage gives the next stage something it needs. If an early stage fails, later stages cannot happen normally.

nodes.label: Enter an address
nodes.detail: The browser reads the URL and works out which site and resource you asked for.

nodes.label: Find the destination
nodes.detail: The browser needs a network address for the named site.

nodes.label: Open a protected path
nodes.detail: The browser and server establish a way to exchange data and, for HTTPS, protect it.

nodes.label: Ask for a resource
nodes.detail: An HTTP request states what the browser wants.

nodes.label: Receive the result
nodes.detail: The server returns an HTTP status, descriptive fields, and usually a body.

nodes.label: Build the page
nodes.detail: The browser reads HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other resources and produces the interface.

sections.title: 1. Pressing Enter starts a round trip
sections.summary: Before learning the protocol names, get the four roles straight: your browser asks, a server answers, and a network carries the exchange.

visual.title: The two ends of the conversation
visual.caption: The browser is the client in this example because it starts the request; the server is the program that receives it and returns an outcome.

nodes.label: Browser · client
nodes.detail: Starts the request, receives resources, and turns them into the page you use.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.detail: Listens for requests, runs application logic, and returns a response.

blocks.text: Imagine entering https://example.com/products/42 and pressing Enter. Your browser cannot simply display a page that lives somewhere else. It first has to identify the destination, reach software at that destination, describe what it wants, receive the result, and then interpret the returned files. That request-and-response conversation is the backbone of ordinary web browsing.

items.title: Client
items.summary: Software that starts a request. In this story, the browser is the client.

items.title: Server
items.summary: Software that waits for requests and returns an outcome.
items.whenToUse: Think 'the side receiving and answering the request.'
items.example: Web server returns HTML or JSON

items.title: Request
items.summary: A message describing what the client wants and any information needed to handle it.

items.title: Response
items.summary: The server's outcome: whether the request worked, descriptive information, and often returned content.

blocks.prompt: If the browser is the client, does that mean all client code runs in a browser?
blocks.explanation: Client means the side that initiates a particular request. A phone app, command-line tool, or another server can also be a client when it asks another service for something.

sections.title: 2. The web address tells the browser where to begin
sections.summary: A URL is a structured address. Its pieces answer different questions instead of acting like one long name.

blocks.text: The technical name for a complete web address is a URL, short for Uniform Resource Locator. In https://example.com/products/42?currency=USD#reviews, the browser can separate the communication scheme, the site name, the resource path, optional query input, and an optional location inside the returned document.

rows: Use the HTTPS rules for this request.
This is the named destination the browser must find on the network.
Ask that destination for this resource or route.
Send optional input as part of the request target.
Move to a location inside the returned document; this fragment is not sent in the HTTP request.
blocks.caption: Read a URL as a set of jobs

blocks.title: Domain name versus URL
blocks.body: A domain name such as example.com can be part of a URL. The URL can additionally contain a scheme, port, path, query, and fragment. Calling the whole address a domain hides useful information when debugging.

blocks.title: The browser may answer locally first
blocks.body: Before using the network, a browser can reuse cached data or involve a service worker, extension, or browser policy. A network request is common, but it is not the only possible path after Enter is pressed.

sections.title: 3. The browser turns the site name into a network destination
sections.summary: People remember names such as example.com; network routing ultimately needs an address it can use to reach a machine or service.

visual.title: From a host name to an address
visual.caption: DNS is the naming step. It does not download the page itself.

nodes.label: Look nearby
nodes.detail: The browser, operating system, or local resolver may already have a valid cached answer.

nodes.label: Ask DNS
nodes.detail: If needed, a DNS resolver finds records for the host name.

nodes.label: Receive an address
nodes.detail: Records such as A or AAAA can provide IPv4 or IPv6 addresses.

nodes.label: Use the answer
nodes.detail: The browser can now try to reach the destination over the network.

blocks.text: DNS, the Domain Name System, is a distributed naming system. The browser needs it because the host name in a URL is convenient for people but is not itself the numeric network address used for IP routing. An IP address identifies where packets can be routed; DNS records help map the host name to that kind of address or to other naming information.

items.title: Reuse a valid answer when possible
items.explanation: DNS answers can be cached by several layers so every visit does not require the full lookup work.
items.result: A still-valid cached address can be used immediately.

items.title: Ask a recursive resolver when needed
items.explanation: A recursive resolver is a DNS service that obtains the answer on the client's behalf, using cached information or following the DNS hierarchy.
items.result: The client receives the relevant DNS records.

items.title: Respect the answer's lifetime
items.explanation: A DNS record can include a time-to-live, or TTL, that limits how long that cached answer may be reused.
items.result: Old but still-valid answers can remain visible until their cache lifetime ends.

blocks.prompt: If DNS cannot provide a usable destination for the host, can that server return an HTTP 404 for this request?
blocks.answer: No — not from that unresolved destination.
blocks.explanation: A 404 is an HTTP response. The browser first needs to reach an HTTP-speaking destination far enough to receive that response. A DNS failure happens earlier in the chain.

sections.title: 4. The browser creates a path for the conversation and protects HTTPS traffic
sections.summary: Reaching an address is not the same as having a safe application conversation. Transport moves data; TLS protects HTTPS communication.

visual.title: Different layers solve different problems
visual.caption: Keeping these jobs separate makes both learning and debugging much easier.

nodes.label: IP routing
nodes.detail: Moves packets across networks toward an address.

nodes.label: Transport
nodes.detail: Provides the communication behavior HTTP uses, such as TCP for common HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connections or QUIC for HTTP/3.

nodes.label: TLS security
nodes.detail: Authenticates the server and protects the confidentiality and integrity of HTTPS data in transit.

nodes.label: HTTP meaning
nodes.detail: Defines what the request and response mean once the communication path exists.

blocks.text: Transport is the part of the networking stack that carries application data with defined delivery behavior. With HTTPS, the browser also establishes TLS, Transport Layer Security. During that security setup, the browser checks the server's certificate and the two sides establish cryptographic keys so later HTTP data can be protected in transit.

rows: Turn a host name into useful naming/address information.
Reach the destination and carry application data.
Timeout, refused connection, reset, unreachable network.
Describe the request and the server's outcome.
blocks.caption: Do not collapse every network problem into 'the internet is broken'

blocks.title: HTTP versions use the layers differently
blocks.body: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP with TLS for HTTPS. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which runs over UDP and integrates transport and cryptographic setup differently. The implementation changes, but the learner-facing question remains the same: can the browser and server exchange protected HTTP messages?

sections.title: 5. HTTP says what the browser wants and what the server decided
sections.summary: Once communication is possible, HTTP gives the exchange a shared structure and meaning.

blocks.text: HTTP, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, defines request and response semantics for the web. A request includes a method that describes the intended operation, a target resource, and fields called headers that add context. A response includes a status code that summarizes the outcome, response headers, and often a body containing HTML, JSON, an image, or another representation of a resource.

blocks.code:
GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html
blocks.explanation: GET says the client wants to retrieve a representation. /products/42 is the request target. Host identifies the named host, and Accept says HTML is an acceptable response format.

blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: max-age=300

<!doctype html>...
blocks.explanation: 200 reports a successful outcome. Content-Type tells the browser how to interpret the body. Cache-Control describes reuse rules. The blank line separates the header section from the HTML body.

items.title: Methods
items.summary: Methods give operations standard meaning: GET retrieves, POST submits data for processing, PUT replaces a known resource representation, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE requests removal.

items.title: Status codes
items.summary: Three digits summarize the outcome. 2xx is successful handling, 3xx redirects, 4xx means the request cannot be fulfilled as sent or authorized, and 5xx reports a server-side failure.

items.title: Headers
items.summary: Named fields carry information about content type, caching, authentication, negotiation, and other handling rules.

blocks.prompt: A server returns 404 Not Found. Which earlier parts of the chain must have worked far enough for you to receive that status?
blocks.answer: The browser reached an HTTP-speaking destination and exchanged enough data to receive an HTTP response.
blocks.explanation: That means the request got past basic name resolution/reachability and, for HTTPS, far enough through protected communication to receive the status. A 404 points you toward the requested route or resource, not toward a simple DNS failure.

sections.title: 6. The browser turns returned resources into the page you see
sections.summary: Receiving HTML is not the finish line. The browser still has to interpret resources, run code, calculate layout, and draw the result.

visual.title: From returned files to pixels
visual.caption: The browser builds internal models first, then calculates and draws the interface.

nodes.label: Parse HTML
nodes.detail: Build the document structure from markup.

nodes.label: Load needed resources
nodes.detail: Request stylesheets, scripts, fonts, images, and other dependencies.

nodes.label: Resolve styles and run scripts
nodes.detail: CSS contributes presentation rules; JavaScript can read or change the page and application state.

nodes.label: Layout
nodes.detail: Calculate the sizes and positions of visible boxes.

nodes.label: Paint and composite
nodes.detail: Draw visual parts and combine layers into the screen output.

blocks.text: As HTML is parsed, the browser creates a tree-like in-memory representation of the document called the DOM, or Document Object Model. CSS rules are resolved against the document, JavaScript can inspect and change the DOM and other browser-managed state, and the browser performs layout, painting, and compositing to produce pixels. These steps can repeat as the page changes.

blocks.title: A fast response can still produce a slow page
blocks.body: Server response time is only one part of perceived speed. Large scripts, blocking resources, expensive layout/paint work, oversized media, and repeated main-thread work can delay what the user can see or use after the server has already answered.

items: Reserve space for media so later loading does not unexpectedly move nearby content.
Reduce work and resources that block the first useful view.
Use caching rules that match how often a resource actually changes.
Measure on realistic devices and network conditions, not only a fast development computer.
Use browser Network, Console, and Performance tools to separate request problems from rendering or JavaScript problems.

sections.title: 7. Debug by finding the earliest stage that failed
sections.summary: A symptom becomes useful when you map it to the first system capable of producing it instead of changing unrelated code.

rows: The browser may not yet know a destination address.
Connection times out or is refused
The destination was named, but a usable communication path was not established.
The browser could not accept the protected identity/security setup.
An HTTP response arrived, so inspect what resource was requested and how the server routes it.
HTML appears but has no styling
The main document arrived; check whether the stylesheet URL loaded and whether the browser accepted it.
Network delivery may be complete while browser execution is still overloaded.
blocks.caption: Use the symptom to choose the first evidence to inspect

items.title: Reproduce the exact request
items.explanation: Use the same URL, account state, browser, and environment when those details matter.
items.result: You know which failure you are actually investigating.

items.title: Find the earliest broken stage
items.explanation: Check the address, naming, connection/security, HTTP result, resource loading, then browser execution in dependency order.
items.result: Later symptoms do not distract you from the first cause.

items.title: Inspect evidence before changing code
items.explanation: Use DNS tools when naming is failing and browser Network/Console/Performance evidence when the failure is in later stages.
items.result: The proposed fix is tied to observed behavior.

items.title: Change one cause and verify the original symptom
items.explanation: A fix is not proven by a different test passing; repeat the request that originally failed.
items.result: You confirm the chain now succeeds where it previously broke.

glossary.definition: A client application that requests web resources, interprets them, runs web code, and presents the resulting interface.
A structured resource address that can contain a scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment.
A human-readable name in the DNS naming system, such as example.com; it can appear as the host part of a URL.
The distributed Domain Name System that provides records for names, including records that map a host name to IP addresses.
An Internet Protocol address used by networks to identify and route toward a network interface or destination.
The communication layer that carries application data with defined delivery behavior, such as TCP or QUIC in common web stacks.
Transport Layer Security, which authenticates peers and protects data in transit for HTTPS.
The web application protocol that defines request and response semantics.
A named HTTP field that carries information used to understand or control request/response handling.
The Document Object Model: the browser's object representation of the document that scripts and browser APIs can inspect and change.
The browser work that converts document, style, script, media, and state into the visual interface.
